the_rules.statement: The noun ato/at (water/bread) is followed directly by the adjective mXe (abundant): the adjective comes after its noun.
The adjective mXe stands right after the noun it qualifies, ato or at; it does not open a phrase on its own.
The noun phrase 'noun + mXe' is closed by a verb: the word after mXe begins with a verbal prefix p-, b- or y-.
When Isis is addressed as woSi (with final -i), the next word is Osiris, also ending in -i (Soreyi, aSoreyi): the two addressed nouns stand side by side with the same ending.
A filiation word (terike-, tedxe- 'begotten by', 'born of') comes directly after the parent's noun phrase, which is a name or else ends in -li or -ye.
The relation word yetmde- ('relative of') comes directly after the noun phrase it governs, closed by a determiner -l/-leb (or -li, -ye) or being a name.
In the offering formulas the verb's stem follows the noun two words before it: after 'ato mXe' the verb has the stem X (ẖe, water), after 'at mXe' it has the stem xr/kr (ḫr, bread).
A verb with the prefix ps- (written pS, piS, peS, bS, ps) stands directly after a word ending in mXe/mxe/mXo: the verb closes its clause right after that word.
The prefix vowel o (pSo-, piSo-, bSo-) appears on a ps- verb almost only when the stem begins with X/x (ẖ); before xr it never occurs.
The verb with the stem Xol (ẖol, formula C) takes the bare prefix p- or no prefix, not the ps- that the water and bread verbs take.
On a ps- verb ending in -te, the stem xr/kr (ḫr) always keeps k before the ending (-kte, -kete), while the stem X (ẖ) often has bare -te (pSiXte).
The first offering formula ('ato mXe' + verb) has before it a word ending in -i, mostly the filiation predicate in -lowi/-qowi or the vocative Soreyi.
When several persons are named (the last filiation word before the verb ends in -bkwi), the benediction verb carries the plural marker -bx(e)- (-bḫe-) before its ending.
the_rules.verdict: not passed: fewer than 20 cases; holds in under 80%

the_rules.statement: Within one text the benediction verbs agree in their final -s: once a verb ends in -kes/-ketes/-ks/-ktes, the next verb also ends in -s.
The vocative invocation woSi (or wiSi) opens the text as its first word.
The second vocative, Soreyi (Osiris), comes right after the invocation of Isis: among the three words before it stands woS/woSi/wiS/wiSi.
The naming clause (a word ending in -qowi, 'this is NN') comes before the filiation clauses (born of / begotten of).
All filiation clauses come before the first benediction (ato/at mXe ...): the benedictions close the descent part and no filiation word follows them.
When a text has both the water benediction (ato mXe ...) and the bread benediction (at mXe ...), the water one comes first.
In a benediction the verb agrees with the object word two places before it: after 'ato mXe' the verb has the stem with X (ẖ), after 'at mXe' it has the stem with xr or kr.
The word right after mXe ('much, plenty') is the verb of the benediction, beginning with the prefix p- (or b-, y-): object and quantifier stand before the verb, verb last.
Benediction verbs (ending in -kete, -kte, -kes, -ketes) stand in their text's latter half.
When the locative ending -te of a place stands inside a word with more letters after it, the next letter is l: the place phrase is closed by the article or copula (-l, -li, -lo, -lowi, -leb).
Words with the verbal ending -kete stand in their text's final third: the benediction formulas close the inscription.
A -kete verb is preceded within two words by its object noun of water or food: a word containing mX/mx or mlo (mXe, xmlol, mlol) or beginning with at (at, ato).
A -kete verb closes its clause: after it the text ends or the next clause begins with a word in a, x or m (at, ato, xmlol, mlo...).
A word beginning with the causative prefix ps- (pS, piS) carries a verbal ending -te, -ke, -kes or -to, on itself or on the next word when the verb is written in two pieces.
Words standing directly beside a numeral carry no suffix: both the counted word in front and the following word are bare stems, without article, case or predicate endings.
the_rules.verdict: not passed: under 30 points above its comparison

the_rules.statement: In the offering list of a text, the item 'ato' comes before the item 'at'.
Each item of the offering list, 'ato' or 'at', has after it a word beginning with m (mostly mXe).
The quantity word mXe/mxe in a list item has after it a verb beginning with p (the causative/verbal prefix p-, mostly pS- or piS-).
The verb of an offering item agrees with the item noun: after 'ato mXe' the verb has X or x but no 'xr'; after 'at mXe' it has 'xr'.
A list item 'at' starts right where the previous item ends: the preceding word is a verb beginning with p or ending in -te or -s.
The word that names the dead person (ending in -qo or -qowi) comes before every filiation and relation clause of the epitaph.
The word just before a filiation predicate (tedxe-lowi 'born of', terike-lowi 'begotten by') names a person: the parent's name stands immediately before the verb of filiation.

A word ending in -leb (plural determiner) directly before a predicate occurs only with the relation verb yetmde, never with the filiation verbs: one has one mother and one father but may have several relatives with a title.
Relation clauses (yetmde-lowi) come after all filiation clauses (mother and father) in a text.
The benediction formulas ('ato/at mXe ...') come after every filiation and relation clause.
In the benediction 'NOUN mXe VERB', the verb after 'ato mXe' (water) carries X (pS(i/o)Xe-kete), the verb after 'at mXe' (bread) carries xr (pS(i)xr-kete).
A filiation predicate in -li (tedxeli, terikeli) is followed at once by the same verb again with its copula (tedxeli tedxelowi, terikeli terikelowi).
When both are present, the maternal filiation (tedxe-) comes before the paternal one (terike-).
the_rules.verdict: not passed: holds in under 80%; under 30 points above its comparison

the_rules.statement: The word after mXe in the offering formula is a prefixed verb: it begins with p, b or y.
When a text has both offering clauses, the 'ato mXe' clause comes before the 'at mXe' clause.
The word just before 'ato mXe' closes a sentence: it ends in -wi, -te or -s.
The parts of the funerary frame come in a fixed order: invocation (woS/wiS), the Sor- word, the name closed by -qowi, the relationship words (teri-, tedx-, tdx-, tereke-), then 'ato mXe'.
The sentence-final ending -wi follows the vowel o in the word: -lowi, -qowi, -towi.
The two offering clauses take different verb roots: after 'ato mXe' the verb contains X (not xr/kr); after 'at mXe' it contains xr or kr.
Two vowel letters (a, e, i, o) are almost never written side by side: where a vowel meets another vowel, as at a stem-ending joint, a glide y or w is written between them.
Where a glide joins two vowels and the later vowel is e or o, that glide is y, not w (w appears mainly in o-w-i).
A word ending in wi has o just before it (-owi): the ending -wi follows the vowel o, with w as the glide.
Word-final -owi is joined only after l, q or t (-lowi, -qowi, -towi): the copula attaches to the determiner l, to qo, or to a t-final stem or ending.
Before the vowel letters i or o, an s or n is written with the plain sign (S, n), never with the syllabic se or ne sign (s, N); so a stem in -se/-ne meeting an i- or o-ending switches sign.
Before a glide y or w, n is written with the ne sign (N), as in -Nyi, unlike before i or o where plain n is used.
The ending kete (also shortened kte) follows a stem ending in r, l or e, e.g. pSixr-kete, Xol-kte, pSiXe-kete.
After a word ending in -se comes a short word of at most three letters, mostly a determiner written apart (l, li, lw or lke) or the copula wi; the -se phrase is closed right after it.
the_rules.verdict: not passed: holds in under 80%; under 30 points above its comparison

the_rules.statement: A word that ends in the letter b has e just before it (-leb, -teb, -seb): the -b that marks the plural follows the vowel e, not another letter.
The sign a stands word-initially only; word-internally and word-finally this sign never writes a vowel.
Two vowel signs never stand side by side: inside a word, e, i or o always has a consonant sign after it.
Inside a word the sign q is followed by o or e far more often than other consonant signs are.
A word ending in -wi has a vowel sign o, e or i just before the w: the copula -wi follows a vowel-final element such as the determiner -lo or qo (-lowi, qowi, -towi).
Inside a word the sign N (ne) has a consonant sign after it, never a vowel sign.
A word that ends in -owi has l, t or q just before it: the ending appears as -lowi, -towi or -qowi.
A word that ends in -wi, without being only wi, has o or e just before it (-owi, -ewi).
A word that ends in b has e just before it: the ending is -eb (as in -leb, -seb, -teb).
Word-final copula -wi comes after the vowel o or e: words end in -owi (-lowi, -towi, -qowi) or -ewi, rarely in a consonant plus -wi.
A word that ends in b has e just before it: the plural ending is written -eb (-leb, -seb, -teb), seldom with another letter before the b.
After a word ending in -se comes a short word of at most three letters, mostly a free-standing ending or particle such as l, li, lw, wi or lke.
the_rules.verdict: not passed: holds in under 80%; under 30 points above its comparison

the_rules.statement: A name that carries an ending does not take an ending beginning with l (the article -l, -li, -lo, -lowi, -leb); names take -te, -i, -qo, -to, -se and the like instead.
A title or other common noun (not a name) that carries the copula -o / -owi has the article l directly before the o: -lo, -lowi, -lw, not bare -o, -to or -qo.

An ending that begins with a vowel (a, e, i, o) is attached only to a stem ending in a consonant sign (woS-i, apedemk-i, pqr-i); after a stem ending in a vowel the ending begins with y instead (Sore-yi, mdewe-yi).
The word ending -owi stands after l or t: words end in -lowi or -towi, almost never in another consonant plus -owi.
A word that ends in -wi has the vowel o or e just before it (-owi, -ewi).
A word written more than once in a text tends to come back inside the same frame: at least one of its neighbours (the word before or the word after) recurs at another of its occurrences.
the_rules.verdict: not passed: holds in under 80%; under 30 points above its comparison
